data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"As n grows, the probability of reaching unanimous consensus tends to 1. Locally stable mixed configurations exist (matching-cuts, per SRC_014) but are dynamically inaccessible: the asynchronous dynamics starting from a uniform random coloring first drives the system to the majority-bias regime where the global magnetization performs a biased walk; on random 3-regular graphs, which are good expanders, the initial imbalance of order sqrt(n) is amplified, and one color wins out before the process can freeze into any matching-cut obstruction. The expected number of obstruction structures reachable from a typical random start is o(1), so consensus probability approaches 1.","counterconditions":[{"case":"The monotonicity of cut size means the process cannot overshoot; if every vertex is stable exactly when it has 2+ same-color neighbors, then any nonzero local minimum of the cut is absorbing and consensus requires reaching cut 0 \u2014 if local minima with \u0398(n) cut are typical endpoints, this claim fails.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the initial magnetization can be zero (exactly balanced random coloring), the amplification mechanism fails on a constant fraction of runs.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If simulation shows terminal cuts with \u0398(n) edges from uniform starts, this claim is falsified.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Coarsening with global bias: a uniform random coloring has magnetization of order sqrt(n) in one color. Each update copies the neighborhood majority, and on an expander the neighborhood majority correlates with the global majority, so the magnetization performs a biased random walk toward fixation. Standard coarsening results (Kanoria\u2013Montanari style) for majority dynamics on dense-enough expanders give fast consensus; degree 3 is marginal but the magnetization bias still dominates because locally stable matching-cuts require an extremely fine global coordination of crossing edges that a trajectory whose cut size is monotonically decreasing through generic states is exponentially unlikely to land on.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
